planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Regina is prized above all for reliable, heavy flowering rather than novel color, so give it the sunniest, driest spot available.

directions: Regina is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection chosen less for a new flower color than for outstanding, dependable garden performance and exceptional cold tolerance among Nerine bowdenii cultivars. Its rose-pink, wavy-petaled, funnel-shaped flowers open in tight terminal umbels on bare stems in early autumn, followed by strappy foliage that persists into winter before dying back for summer dormancy. Compared with the taller, larger-flowered 'Zeal Giant' and 'Pink Triumph', Regina keeps a noticeably compact habit that suits small borders and pot culture, and it has proven reliably free-flowering even after cold, wet winters. In Gulf Coast zone 8-10 gardens, plant in the hottest, driest spot available and withhold water completely during summer dormancy; leave established clumps undisturbed for several years, since flowering improves as bulbs become congested.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light part shade; named for the Tugela River in South Africa, this Eddie Welsh hybrid is bred for cut-flower substance and holds up well in vase arrangements.

directions: Tugela Ruby emerges with leaves flushed heavily purple, maturing to a glossy green backdrop that sets off its dramatic, thick, maroon-red flower spikes rising to about two feet starting in late summer. Each spike is densely packed with ivory-white starry flowers accented by a distinct purple center, a striking two-tone effect that differs from the all-burgundy foliage-and-flower scheme of 'Sparkling Burgundy' and the compact deep-maroon look of 'Oakhurst'. The long-lasting flower spikes are prized as cut flowers and continue to look good as they set ruby-red seed later in the season. In Gulf Coast gardens the bulbs are reliably hardy in zones 7-10 with a dry mulch over winter; where marginal, lift and store like dahlia tubers.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after danger of frost has passed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bred for the cut-flower trade, Reuben also performs well in borders and large containers.

directions: Reuben opens dark, near-black purple buds that unfurl into dense racemes of starry rose-pink flowers, a softer pastel-toned bloom color that reads quite differently from the maroon-and-ivory spikes of 'Tugela Ruby' or the wine-purple foliage of 'Sparkling Burgundy'. Flowers open from the bottom of the spike upward over several weeks in mid to late summer, rich in nectar and popular with pollinators, and the plant's purple-flushed foliage adds interest before bloom. In zone 7-10 Gulf Coast gardens the bulbs can overwinter in the ground under a thick mulch; in colder or wetter areas lift after foliage yellows, cure, and store dry over winter like other tender summer bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a green-and-white sibling of 'Tugela Ruby', also bred for the cut-flower market.

directions: Tugela Jade stands apart from its purple- and burgundy-toned Eucomis comosa siblings by opening chartreuse-green buds into dense racemes of clean, pure white starry flowers, giving a crisp green-and-white look rather than the wine and maroon tones of 'Sparkling Burgundy', 'Oakhurst', 'Tugela Ruby', and 'Reuben'. Named for the Tugela River in South Africa, it blooms in mid to late summer with long-lasting, nectar-rich spikes that are excellent as cut flowers and continue opening from the bottom up for weeks. Grow in full sun in evenly moist, well-drained soil; in Gulf Coast zone 7-10 gardens the bulbs generally overwinter outdoors under mulch, but lift and store dry where winters run colder or wetter than the plant tolerates.

common_name: Sunset in Oz Tiger Flower (Flame-Streaked Peacock Tiger Flower)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60F; a specialty selection sourced mainly through bulb-society exchanges and small nurseries rather than mass Dutch bulb catalogs.

directions: Sunset in Oz arose as a chance seedling selected by nurserywoman Ellen Hornig at Seneca Hill Perennials in Oswego, New York, and was named for the fiery lakeside sunsets there. Rather than the flat, solid marigold-orange of the species or the clean pastel tones of cultivars like 'Rosea' or 'Lilacea', its three-petaled flowers carry streaks and washes of red flaming out over a marigold base, giving each bloom a more variegated, painterly look. As with all Tigridia, each flower lasts only a single day but a well-grown clump produces a long summer-into-fall succession of buds. In Gulf Coast gardens treat exactly like the species: dig and dry the corms after foliage dies back if winters run colder than zone 8, and store in a cool, frost-free spot until spring replanting.

common_name: Mabel Corn Lily (Deep Magenta Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Mabel is a Dutch-bred corn lily hybrid carrying star-shaped flowers in a richer, more saturated deep magenta-pink than the clear rose of 'Rose Queen', each bloom deepening toward a dark, almost blackish-purple center eye. Upright wiry stems hold long-lasting flowers that, like all Ixia, close in overcast weather and open fully only in strong sun, so give it the brightest spot available and plant in generous drifts of 25 or more for impact. Allow foliage to yellow and die back completely after bloom before removing it, and in Gulf Coast gardens with humid summers, lift the corms and store them dry until fall to avoid rot during the required dry dormancy.

common_name: Panorama Corn Lily (Rosy-Pink Dark-Eyed Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Panorama bears loose, wiry spikes of rosy-pink, star-shaped flowers with a slightly darker eye, a softer and more delicate bicolor effect than the intensely saturated magenta of 'Mabel' or the fiery red-orange of 'Vulcan'. Individual stems can carry up to twenty flowers that open flat and shining in full sun but remain cupped shut on overcast days, so a bright, open site is essential for a full display. Massed in drifts above the grasslike foliage, Panorama makes an excellent long-lasting cut flower. In Gulf Coast gardens grow it exactly like other Ixia hybrids: allow the foliage to die back fully after bloom, and lift and store the corms dry over summer where rainfall is heavy enough to risk rot during dormancy.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free areas (zones 9-10) or start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost in cold climates; a long-grown bicolor freesia cultivar valued for its warm sunset coloring.

directions: Oberon is a bicolor freesia cultivar with a golden-yellow flower base flushed orange to vermilion along the outer edges of each petal, giving the fragrant, funnel-shaped blooms a warm, sunset-like gradient quite different from the solid clear yellow of 'Rijnveld's Golden Yellow' or the pure white of 'Ballerina'. Flowers are carried on the same slender, arching, wiry stems and narrow sword-shaped foliage typical of florists' freesias, and the strong sweet scent carries well indoors as a cut flower. Stems benefit from twiggy brush or a grow-through support to stay upright. In frost-free Gulf Coast gardens the corms are perennial and can be left in the ground; elsewhere lift after foliage yellows, dry thoroughly, and store cool and dry until fall replanting.
